country.name: Washington
country.summary: Washington is on most counts the second wine state of the Union by volume, and almost none of its wine is made where it rains. The Cascade Range splits the state: Seattle and Puget Sound on the wet western side, and the Columbia basin to the east, a near desert in the mountains' rain shadow where 150 to 200 millimetres (six to eight inches) fall in a year and every vine drinks from a drip line. The Columbia Valley AVA of 1984 covers that basin and holds nearly every vineyard in the state, with the Yakima Valley, Red Mountain, the Walla Walla Valley, the Horse Heaven Hills and the rest nested inside it. Cabernet Sauvignon leads, Merlot and Syrah follow, Riesling and Chardonnay head the whites, and most of the vines stand on their own roots. Washington adds nothing to federal label law; its traps are geography.
country.overview:
Vines reached the state early and wine came late. The Hudson's Bay Company planted grapes at Fort Vancouver in 1825, Italian settlers grew them around Walla Walla in the 1870s, and irrigation canals opened the Yakima Valley to orchards and Concord grapes from the start of the twentieth century. Prohibition and then a state monopoly on liquor kept the industry to sweet fortified wines until the 1960s, when a group of university professors founded Associated Vintners, later Columbia Winery, in 1962 to make dry vinifera wine, and a Seattle company that would become Chateau Ste. Michelle took the Napa consultant André Tchelistcheff on in 1967 and put the Ste. Michelle name on its first vinifera bottlings that year. Ste. Michelle built its château at Woodinville, west of the mountains and near the city, in 1976, which is why so many Washington wineries sit a mountain pass away from their vines. Leonetti Cellar opened in Walla Walla in 1977, Woodward Canyon in 1981, L'Ecole No 41 in 1983; the Yakima Valley became the state's first AVA in 1983 and the Columbia Valley followed in 1984.

The geography is a single fact with many consequences. Pacific storms drop their rain on the Cascades, so the Columbia basin east of them is shrub-steppe with long, hot, dry summers, cold winters, and summer days at 46 to 47 degrees north that run longer than California's. Ice-age floods from glacial Lake Missoula spread sand, silt and gravel across the basalt, and windblown loess settled on top; the soils drain fast, carry little organic matter and host little phylloxera, so most vines are own-rooted. Irrigation is a tool as much as a necessity: the grower decides how much water the vine gets and when. The cost is winter, when an arctic freeze every several years kills buds and trunks, and own-rooted vines are retrained from the ground. West of the Cascades, Puget Sound is the one AVA on the wet side, cool enough only for early-ripening grapes. The Columbia Gorge straddles the river into Oregon and is a separate AVA from the Columbia Valley; the Lewis-Clark Valley is shared with Idaho.

The law is federal and only federal: 75 per cent of the named grape, 85 per cent from a named AVA, 95 per cent from a stated vintage on an AVA wine. The one twist is a shared AVA. The Walla Walla Valley crosses into Oregon, and The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater lies wholly on the Oregon side, so a Washington-made wine from its cobbles may say Walla Walla Valley but not The Rocks District, because an AVA name may be used only on wine fully finished in a state the AVA touches.

The exam leans on the rain shadow, the Columbia Valley as umbrella, Yakima as the first AVA, Red Mountain for Cabernet, Walla Walla and the Rocks for Syrah, Chateau Ste. Michelle for Riesling, own-rooted vines, and the state's second place in American production.
ladder: The state appellation: 75 per cent of the grapes from Washington under federal law; the state adds no stricter rule.
The umbrella AVA of 1984 covering the basin east of the Cascades and reaching into Oregon; the label a blend across the nested AVAs wears.

The working appellations inside the Columbia Valley: Yakima Valley, Walla Walla Valley, Red Mountain, Horse Heaven Hills, Wahluke Slope, Ancient Lakes, Lake Chelan and the rest; 85 per cent of the grapes from the named area.
Red Mountain, Rattlesnake Hills, Snipes Mountain, Candy Mountain and Goose Gap sit inside the Yakima Valley inside the Columbia Valley; The Rocks District sits inside the Walla Walla Valley.
Puget Sound west of the Cascades, the Columbia Gorge along the river into Oregon, and the Lewis-Clark Valley shared with Idaho.
No legal meaning in Washington or anywhere in the United States.
labels: The umbrella AVA; on a label it usually means grapes drawn from several nested areas.
The AVA of 1984 shared with Oregon; the name a Rocks District wine finished in Washington must use.
The small, warm AVA of 2001 near Benton City; Cabernet Sauvignon of weight and tannin.
Chateau Ste. Michelle's Riesling made with the Mosel house Dr. Loosen since 1999; a proper noun, not a style term.
The trademarked American term, used under licence, for a blend of two or more Bordeaux grapes with none above 90 per cent; coined for blends that could not carry a varietal name.
Federal: every grape from vineyards the winery owns or controls inside the named AVA, the wine made and bottled there.
The name Washington has long used for Blaufränkisch.
The only Washington AVA west of the Cascades, approved in 1995: Madeleine Angevine, Siegerrebe and Müller-Thurgau.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The most planted grape: ripe cassis and black cherry with firm tannin and fresh acidity from the cold nights, finest on Red Mountain, in the Horse Heaven Hills and in Walla Walla.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The grape that first made the state's reputation, firmer and darker here than in California; a varietal wine and the partner in Bordeaux blends.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Dark, peppery and meaty, at its most distinctive on the basalt cobbles of The Rocks District in the Walla Walla Valley.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Grown at scale in the Yakima Valley and the Ancient Lakes: dry and off-dry wines of lime and white peach, Chateau Ste. Michelle's Eroica the reference.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The most planted white in many counts, from large-scale fresh styles to barrel-fermented wines from the cooler northern sites.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: A blending grape in the Bordeaux-style wines and an occasional perfumed varietal.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: A small but prized planting in Walla Walla and the Columbia Valley, inky and blended or bottled alone.

grapes.name: Blaufränkisch
grapes.styles: Sold as Lemberger, a peppery, bright red that Washington has grown since the 1970s.

exam: Say the geography first: the Cascades' rain shadow, 150 to 200 millimetres (six to eight inches) of rain, irrigation on every vine, nearly all vineyards east of the mountains.
Hold the dates: Yakima Valley 1983 as the first AVA, Columbia Valley 1984, Walla Walla Valley 1984, Puget Sound 1995, Red Mountain 2001.
Know which AVAs are not inside the Columbia Valley: Puget Sound, Columbia Gorge, Lewis-Clark Valley.
Carry the federal percentages, 75 varietal, 85 AVA, 95 vintage, and know that Washington adds nothing to them.
Pair the grapes with their places: Cabernet with Red Mountain and the Horse Heaven Hills, Syrah with the Rocks District, Riesling with the Ancient Lakes and Ste. Michelle.
Explain own-rooted vines in one line: sandy flood soils, cold winters and isolation have kept phylloxera rare.
traps: Seattle's rain never reaches the vines; the Columbia Valley is a desert, and the wet side has one AVA, Puget Sound.
Columbia Valley and Columbia Gorge are different AVAs; the Gorge is not inside the Valley, though both reach into Oregon.
The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater is in Oregon; a Washington-finished wine may say Walla Walla Valley but not the Rocks.
Washington is counted second in American wine production after California; New York is usually third and Oregon fourth.
Washington has no 90 per cent rule; that is Oregon's. Washington follows the federal 75.
Woodinville is a winery town, not a vineyard: the grapes are trucked over the Cascades from the Columbia Valley.

cards.f: Why the Columbia Valley is a desert
cards.b: The Cascade Range wrings Pacific storms out on its western slopes; the basin east of it gets 150 to 200 millimetres (six to eight inches) of rain a year and every vineyard is irrigated.

cards.f: Washington's latitude: what it gives the vine
cards.b: About 46 to 47 degrees north: summer days run about two hours longer than California's, so grapes ripen fully while the cold desert nights keep their acidity.

cards.f: The Washington AVAs outside the Columbia Valley
cards.b: Puget Sound (1995) west of the Cascades; Columbia Gorge (2004) along the river into Oregon; Lewis-Clark Valley (2016) shared with Idaho.

cards.f: Why so many Washington vines are own-rooted
cards.b: Deep, sandy, free-draining flood soils, cold winters and isolation have kept phylloxera rare; a frozen trunk is retrained from its own roots, with no graft to lose.
Second by volume after California on most counts; New York is usually third and Oregon fourth.

cards.f: The Rocks District: the label rule
cards.b: Wholly in Oregon inside the Walla Walla Valley AVA. An AVA name goes only on wine fully finished in a state the AVA touches, so a Washington-finished wine says Walla Walla Valley instead.

cards.f: Chateau Ste. Michelle: why a sommelier knows it
cards.b: Washington's founding large house, its château built at Woodinville west of the Cascades in 1976; by most counts the largest Riesling producer in the world, and maker of Eroica with Dr. Loosen of the Mosel from 1999.

cards.f: Washington's leading grapes, red and white
cards.b: Cabernet Sauvignon first, then Merlot and Syrah; Chardonnay and Riesling lead the whites.

questions.q: Which Washington AVA lies west of the Cascade Range?
questions.exp: Puget Sound, approved in 1995, is the one AVA on the wet western side and grows early-ripening grapes. The Columbia Gorge straddles the river, Lake Chelan and Yakima lie east.

questions.q: Where does Washington rank among American states by volume of wine produced?
questions.exp: Washington stands second after California on most counts of volume, with New York usually third and Oregon fourth.

questions.q: Which Washington house created Eroica Riesling with the Mosel estate Dr. Loosen in 1999?
questions.exp: Chateau Ste. Michelle of Woodinville made the first Eroica in 1999 with Dr. Loosen of the Mosel, a taut Riesling in the Mosel manner; the house is by most counts the largest Riesling producer in the world.

questions.q: Which house, founded in 1977, was the Walla Walla Valley's first modern winery?
questions.exp: Leonetti Cellar was first in 1977; Woodward Canyon followed in 1981, L'Ecole No 41 in 1983 and Cayuse in 1997.

questions.q: Which AVA does Washington share with Idaho?
questions.exp: The Lewis-Clark Valley of 2016 crosses into Idaho. The Snake River Valley is Idaho and Oregon; the Columbia Gorge and Walla Walla Valley are shared with Oregon.

questions.q: Under which name has Washington long grown and sold Blaufränkisch?
questions.exp: Washington has grown Blaufränkisch as Lemberger since the 1970s, a bright, peppery red. The name is German; the grape is a vinifera, not a hybrid, and nothing to do with Limburger cheese.

questions.q: What minimum share of the named grape must a Washington varietal wine contain?
questions.exp: Washington adds nothing to the federal floor of 75 per cent of the named grape. The 90 per cent rule is Oregon's; 85 per cent is the federal AVA floor and 95 the vintage floor.

regions.name: Columbia Valley (WA)
regions.summary: The Columbia Valley is nearly all of Washington's wine: a vast AVA of 1984 east of the Cascades, in the mountains' rain shadow, where 150 to 200 millimetres (six to eight inches) of rain fall a year and every vine is irrigated. It crosses into Oregon and holds the state's working appellations: the Yakima Valley, Washington's first AVA of 1983, Red Mountain, the Walla Walla Valley, the Horse Heaven Hills and the Wahluke Slope. Cabernet Sauvignon is the most planted grape, Merlot and Syrah follow, and Riesling and Chardonnay lead the whites. The vines stand on windblown loess and flood sands over basalt, most on their own roots, and the long summer days of 46 degrees north ripen them fully.

terroir.climate: Continental semi-desert in the rain shadow of the Cascades: most of the basin sees 150 to 200 millimetres (six to eight inches) of rain a year, so irrigation is compulsory. Summers are hot and dry with cool nights, a swing that keeps acidity in ripe fruit, and at 46 to 47 degrees north the summer days run about two hours longer than California's. Winters are cold, and every several years an arctic freeze kills buds and trunks. Humidity and disease pressure are low. Harvest runs from September into late October.
terroir.soils: Columbia River basalt, the flood lavas of the plateau, lies under everything. On it sit the sands, silts and gravels left by the Missoula Floods, the ice-age torrents that burst from a glacial lake in Montana and swept the basin, and over them windblown loess. The result is deep, free-draining, low-fertility, alkaline soil in which phylloxera has never prospered, so most vines are own-rooted. Red Mountain's sandy soil is lime-rich and high in pH; The Rocks District is a fan of basalt cobbles; the Yakima and Walla Walla valleys carry silt loams.
terroir.topography: A basin of ridges and slopes between the Cascades and the Blue Mountains, from the Okanogan highlands south to the Oregon line. Vineyards take the south-facing slopes of basalt folds, the Rattlesnake Hills, the Saddle Mountains, the Horse Heaven Hills, and the benches above the Columbia, Yakima and Snake rivers, mostly between about 150 and 610 metres (500 and 2,000 feet). The Walla Walla Valley rises eastward to the foothills of the Blue Mountains.
terroir.water: The Columbia and its tributaries, the Yakima, the Snake and the Walla Walla, cut the basin and feed its canals and drip lines; the great river moderates the Horse Heaven Hills and the Wahluke Slope, whose vineyards look down on it. Lake Chelan, deep and glacial, tempers the northernmost AVA.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The most planted grape and the state's flagship: cassis, black cherry and graphite, firm tannin, fresh acidity from the cold nights; Red Mountain, the Horse Heaven Hills and Walla Walla are the names.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The grape that built the reputation in the 1980s and 1990s, darker and firmer than California's, as a varietal and in Bordeaux-style blends.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Dark fruit, pepper, smoked meat and olive; savoury and almost funky from the cobbles of The Rocks District, riper and plusher from the Wahluke Slope.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Grown at scale for dry and off-dry wines of lime, white peach and wet stone, best from the cooler Ancient Lakes and Yakima sites.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: A large planting across the basin, from fresh unoaked wines to barrel-fermented bottlings from the cooler northern benches.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: A blending partner in the Bordeaux-style wines and a perfumed varietal from a few houses.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: Inky and floral, a small planting that Walla Walla houses prize for blends and single bottlings.

grapes.name: Petit Verdot
grapes.styles: A seasoning grape in the Bordeaux blends, ripening fully in the long, dry summers.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: Part of the Rhône-style blends of Walla Walla and the Yakima Valley.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre / Monastrell
grapes.styles: The third grape of the Rhône blends, grown on the warmest slopes.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: A perfumed white from the warm sites, alone or co-fermented with Syrah.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: An aromatic white with a long history in the Yakima Valley, off-dry and lychee-scented.

grapes.name: Blaufränkisch
grapes.styles: Grown as Lemberger since the 1970s: bright, peppery red from the Yakima Valley.

wines.note: Cassis, black cherry and cocoa with firm tannin and bright acidity, usually blended across several nested AVAs. With steak, lamb or a rich stew.
Denser and more tannic than the valley blend, black fruit and dust, built for a decade. The state's answer to Napa's mountain wines; decant and serve with beef.
Blackberry, pepper, olive and smoked meat, savoury rather than sweet. With duck, lamb or grilled sausage.
The most distinctive wine in the state: funky, meaty, floral, iron and olive over dark fruit, grown on basalt cobbles. Pour it for the guest who asks what is unusual.
Plum and black cherry with more grip than California Merlot; the grape that made Washington's name. With roast pork, duck or a burger.
Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Malbec and Petit Verdot in varying shares, often labelled with a proprietary name or Meritage. With prime rib.
Lime, peach and wet stone, dry to off-dry, light and refreshing. With spiced dishes, crab or a first course.
Apple and pear with gentle oak, fuller in the warm south, fresher from the cooler north. With roast chicken or cream sauces.

made.viticulture: Water is the first decision. With 150 to 200 millimetres (a few inches) of rain a year the vine lives on drip irrigation from the Columbia's canals, and growers use deficit irrigation, withholding water after fruit set to shrink the berries and concentrate the wine, a control no rain-fed region has. Most vines are own-rooted: the deep flood sands, the cold winters and the basin's isolation have kept phylloxera rare, though it was confirmed in Walla Walla vineyards in 2019 and new plantings are more often grafted. The hazard is winter. An arctic freeze every several years kills buds and splits trunks, so growers plant on slopes for cold-air drainage, keep two trunks as insurance, and after a freeze retrain an own-rooted vine from its own suckers, with no graft to lose. Training is vertical shoot positioning on bilateral cordons, with wide rows and machine harvesting on the large estates that supply most of the state's wineries under contract. Long summer days and cool nights ripen Cabernet Sauvignon fully while holding acidity, and harvest runs from early September for whites into late October for the last Cabernet.
made.winemaking: The model is Bordeaux for the reds and the Mosel for Riesling. Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot are fermented in stainless or small open tanks, pressed to French and some American oak, and the top wines spend eighteen to twenty two months in barrel with a high share new; Bordeaux-style blends are assembled across the nested AVAs and labelled Columbia Valley when the fruit crosses more than one. Syrah is made more gently in Walla Walla, with whole clusters, concrete and older barrels, so that the Rocks District's savoury character shows. Riesling is fermented cool in stainless steel and often stopped with residual sugar for an off-dry style; Chateau Ste. Michelle's Eroica, made with the Mosel house Dr. Loosen since 1999, set the benchmark for a taut, Mosel-influenced style with a touch of sweetness. Chardonnay runs from unoaked to barrel-fermented.

law.classification: The Columbia Valley AVA was approved in 1984, a year after the Yakima Valley, the state's first. It covers about 4.5 million hectares (eleven million acres), about a quarter of the state, reaches across the river into Oregon, and holds nearly every vineyard in the state. Inside it nest the working appellations, the Yakima Valley and the Walla Walla Valley with their own nested AVAs, the Horse Heaven Hills, the Wahluke Slope and a dozen more. Puget Sound, the Columbia Gorge and the Lewis-Clark Valley are Washington AVAs outside it. Every AVA states origin only, and Washington adds no rule of its own to the federal floors: 75 per cent of the named grape, 85 per cent from a named AVA, 95 per cent from a stated vintage. An AVA's name may be used only on wine fully finished in a state the AVA touches, which keeps the Rocks District off Washington-made labels.
tiers: The state appellation: 75 per cent of the grapes from Washington under federal law.
The umbrella AVA of 1984, 85 per cent of the grapes from inside it; the label for blends drawn from several nested areas.

Yakima Valley, Walla Walla Valley, Horse Heaven Hills, Wahluke Slope, Ancient Lakes of Columbia Valley, Lake Chelan, Naches Heights, Royal Slope, White Bluffs, The Burn of Columbia Valley, Rocky Reach, Beverly and Columbia Hills: 85 per cent from the named area.
Red Mountain, Rattlesnake Hills, Snipes Mountain, Candy Mountain and Goose Gap within the Yakima Valley; The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater within the Walla Walla Valley.
A named vineyard such as Champoux, Ciel du Cheval or Klipsun: the house's own claim, not a legal tier.
labels: The umbrella; the label a cross-AVA blend wears.
The shared AVA of 1984; the name a Washington-finished Rocks District wine must use.
The warm AVA of 2001 inside the Yakima Valley; Cabernet Sauvignon of weight.
Chateau Ste. Michelle's Riesling with Dr. Loosen since 1999.
The trademarked term for a Bordeaux-style blend; a licence, not a law.
Federal: grapes from the winery's own or controlled vineyards in the AVA, made and bottled there.

places.name: Yakima Valley
places.note: Washington's first AVA, 1983, along the Yakima River from Yakima to the Tri-Cities: the state's oldest vinifera plantings, Riesling, Chardonnay, Merlot and Cabernet beside the hop fields. It holds five AVAs of its own.

places.name: Red Mountain
places.note: A small south-west-facing slope near Benton City, approved in 2001, the warmest ground in the state and among the windiest. Lime-rich, high-pH sand gives Cabernet Sauvignon of dense tannin and dark fruit; Ciel du Cheval and Klipsun are its famous vineyards, Kiona planted the first vines in 1975, and Col Solare built here.

places.name: Rattlesnake Hills
places.note: The ridge north of the Yakima Valley floor around Zillah, approved in 2006: higher, slightly cooler sites for Cabernet, Merlot and Riesling.

places.name: Snipes Mountain
places.note: A small basalt hill near Sunnyside, approved in 2009, with some of the state's oldest vines on its slopes.

places.name: Candy Mountain and Goose Gap
places.note: Two small AVAs of 2020 and 2021 beside Red Mountain, continuing its line of hills towards the Tri-Cities with Cabernet and Syrah.

places.name: Walla Walla Valley
places.note: Approved in 1984 and shared with Oregon, a valley of wheat and onions rising east to the Blue Mountains, with more rain than the basin and deep loess. Leonetti Cellar (1977), Woodward Canyon (1981) and L'Ecole No 41 (1983) made it the state's prestige address for Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah.

places.name: The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater
places.note: Approved in 2015 on the Oregon side: the alluvial fan of the Walla Walla River paved with fist-sized basalt cobbles that store heat and drain fast. Syrah here is savoury, meaty and floral, unlike any other in the state; Cayuse made its name. A Washington-finished wine may not use the name.

places.name: Horse Heaven Hills
places.note: The long south-facing slope between the Yakima Valley and the Columbia, approved in 2005: windy, warm and dry, moderated by the river below. Champoux Vineyard, Quilceda Creek's source, is here, and Columbia Crest at Paterson is one of the state's largest wineries.

places.name: Wahluke Slope
places.note: A broad, warm, south-facing slope north of the Columbia near Mattawa, approved in 2006, among the driest and warmest ground in the state: ripe Merlot, Syrah and Cabernet in volume.

places.name: Ancient Lakes of Columbia Valley
places.note: A cool northern AVA of 2012 around Quincy and George, pocked with the lakes the Missoula Floods carved; Riesling, Chardonnay and other whites of high acidity.

places.name: Lake Chelan
places.note: The northernmost AVA, approved in 2009, on the benches above a deep glacial lake that softens winter and summer alike; aromatic whites and Pinot Noir beside the resort town.

places.name: Naches Heights
places.note: A high basalt plateau west of Yakima, approved in 2012, on volcanic soils rather than flood sediment; small and cool.

places.name: Royal Slope, White Bluffs, The Burn and Rocky Reach
places.note: Four AVAs of 2020 to 2022 in the central and northern basin, from the Royal Slope south of the Ancient Lakes to Rocky Reach on the river north of Wenatchee.

places.name: Beverly and Columbia Hills
places.note: Two AVAs of the 2020s: Beverly, approved in 2024 on the Columbia in Grant County, and Columbia Hills, approved in 2026 in Klickitat County on the river's north bank, both inside the Columbia Valley.

places.name: Woodinville
places.note: Not an AVA but the winery town north-east of Seattle, west of the Cascades, where Chateau Ste. Michelle built in 1976 and scores of producers followed with grapes trucked over the passes.

producers.name: Chateau Ste. Michelle
producers.why: The state's largest and founding house, in Woodinville since 1976, the Riesling benchmark with Eroica and the parent of Columbia Crest and Col Solare.

producers.name: Quilceda Creek
producers.why: A Snohomish family house since 1978 whose Columbia Valley Cabernet Sauvignon from Champoux and its own vineyards earned the state's first perfect scores.

producers.name: Leonetti Cellar
producers.why: Walla Walla's first modern winery, 1977, whose Cabernet and Merlot made the valley a prestige address.

producers.name: Woodward Canyon Winery
producers.why: Walla Walla's second house, 1981, known for Old Vines Cabernet Sauvignon and a serious Chardonnay.

producers.name: L'Ecole No 41
producers.why: Founded in 1983 in the old Frenchtown schoolhouse at Lowden; Bordeaux-style blends and Sémillon from the Walla Walla Valley.

producers.name: Cayuse Vineyards
producers.why: The house that planted the Rocks District's cobbles from 1997 and made its savoury, biodynamically farmed Syrah a cult.

producers.name: Columbia Crest
producers.why: Ste. Michelle's Horse Heaven Hills winery at Paterson since the 1980s, a volume leader and a reliable by-the-glass Cabernet and Merlot.

producers.name: Columbia Winery
producers.why: Founded as Associated Vintners in 1962 by university professors, the first house to bottle dry vinifera wine in the state.

producers.name: Col Solare
producers.why: The Red Mountain estate founded in 1995 by Chateau Ste. Michelle and Antinori of Tuscany; a Cabernet-led blend.

producers.name: DeLille Cellars
producers.why: A Woodinville house since 1992 whose Bordeaux-style blends from Red Mountain and Yakima vineyards set the modern style.

producers.name: Kiona Vineyards
producers.why: Planted Red Mountain's first vines in 1975 and still farms its oldest blocks, including the Lemberger the state grew early.

producers.name: Hedges Family Estate
producers.why: A Red Mountain estate since 1987, farmed biodynamically, whose Cabernet blends show the AVA's tannin and dust.

producers.name: Gramercy Cellars
producers.why: A Walla Walla house built on restrained, savoury Syrah in the northern Rhône manner.

producers.name: Long Shadows Vintners
producers.why: A Walla Walla project from 2003 pairing Columbia Valley fruit with visiting winemakers from Bordeaux, Germany, Australia and California.

exam: Lead with the rain shadow: 150 to 200 millimetres (six to eight inches) of rain, irrigation everywhere, nearly every vineyard east of the Cascades.
Know the umbrella and its first child: Columbia Valley 1984, Yakima Valley 1983; Walla Walla 1984, Red Mountain 2001, Horse Heaven Hills 2005.
Place the grapes: Cabernet on Red Mountain and the Horse Heaven Hills, Syrah in Walla Walla and the Rocks, Riesling in the Ancient Lakes and Yakima.
Explain the Missoula Floods and the loess in one line, and why own-rooted vines follow from them.
Hold the Rocks District rule: in Oregon, inside Walla Walla, off a Washington-finished label.
Name the houses: Chateau Ste. Michelle, Quilceda Creek, Leonetti, Woodward Canyon, L'Ecole No 41, Cayuse.
traps: Yakima Valley, not Columbia Valley, was the first Washington AVA; the umbrella came a year later.
Red Mountain is a slope near Benton City inside the Yakima Valley, not a mountain and not a separate region.
Walla Walla is cooler and wetter than Red Mountain, with loess rather than flood sand; the Rocks' cobbles are its own alluvial fan.
The Rocks District is an Oregon AVA; its wines are discussed with Washington because the Walla Walla Valley is shared.
Washington's own-rooted vines are a soil and climate story, not a law; Oregon's 90 per cent rule is the law story.
Lemberger is Blaufränkisch under a Washington name, not a hybrid and nothing to do with Limburger cheese.
Puget Sound and the Columbia Gorge are Washington AVAs but not inside the Columbia Valley.

cards.f: Columbia Valley AVA: year, size, reach
cards.b: Approved 1984; about 4.5 million hectares (eleven million acres), about a quarter of Washington; crosses into Oregon; holds nearly every vineyard in the state.

cards.f: Washington's first AVA and its year
cards.b: Yakima Valley, 1983, a year before the Columbia Valley umbrella.

cards.f: The Missoula Floods: what they left
cards.b: Ice-age floods from glacial Lake Missoula spread sand, silt and gravel over the basalt; windblown loess settled on top. Deep, free-draining, alkaline, phylloxera-poor soils.
AVA of 2001 near Benton City inside the Yakima Valley; the state's warmest slope, and windy; lime-rich sand; dense Cabernet Sauvignon; Ciel du Cheval and Klipsun; Col Solare.

cards.f: The Rocks District: soil, wine, state
cards.b: Basalt cobbles on the Walla Walla River's alluvial fan; savoury, meaty Syrah; wholly in Oregon inside the Walla Walla Valley AVA; approved 2015.
Leonetti Cellar 1977, Woodward Canyon 1981, L'Ecole No 41 in 1983.
Withholding drip water after fruit set to shrink berries and concentrate flavour; possible only because the basin's 150 to 200 millimetres of rain leave the grower in control.

cards.f: The Columbia Valley's nested AVAs of 2020 and after
cards.b: Royal Slope and Candy Mountain 2020; Goose Gap, White Bluffs and The Burn 2021; Rocky Reach 2022; Beverly 2024; Columbia Hills 2026.

cards.f: Washington's winter hazard and the grower's answer
cards.b: An arctic freeze every several years kills buds and trunks; growers plant on slopes for cold-air drainage, keep two trunks, and retrain own-rooted vines from their suckers.

questions.q: Which pest's rarity in the sandy flood soils lets most Columbia Valley vines grow on their own roots?
questions.exp: Phylloxera has never prospered in the basin's deep, sandy, free-draining soils and cold winters, so most vines are own-rooted. It was confirmed in Walla Walla vineyards in 2019, and new plantings are more often grafted.

questions.q: Which was Washington's first AVA, approved in 1983?
questions.exp: The Yakima Valley was first in 1983. Walla Walla followed in 1984, Red Mountain in 2001 and the Horse Heaven Hills in 2005.

questions.q: Which mountain range's rain shadow makes the Columbia Valley a near desert?
questions.exp: Pacific storms drop their rain on the western slopes of the Cascades; the Columbia basin east of them receives 150 to 200 millimetres (six to eight inches) a year and is irrigated throughout.

questions.q: Which AVA near Benton City is Washington's benchmark for dense, tannic Cabernet Sauvignon?
questions.exp: Red Mountain, approved in 2001 inside the Yakima Valley, is a warm, windy slope of lime-rich sand. Rattlesnake Hills and Snipes Mountain are other Yakima Valley AVAs; Naches Heights is a cool plateau west of Yakima.

questions.q: Which AVA nested in the Columbia Valley crosses the state line into Oregon?
questions.exp: The Walla Walla Valley AVA of 1984 lies on both sides of the line and holds The Rocks District on the Oregon side. The Horse Heaven Hills, the Wahluke Slope and the Yakima Valley lie wholly in Washington.

questions.q: Which soil feature marks the vineyards of The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater?
questions.exp: The Rocks District is the Walla Walla River's alluvial fan, paved with fist-sized basalt cobbles that store heat and drain fast. Loess blankets much of the basin, red volcanic clay is Oregon's Jory, and chalk belongs to Champagne.

questions.q: Which grape is the most planted in Washington?
questions.exp: Cabernet Sauvignon leads the state's plantings, with Merlot and Syrah behind it among the reds; Chardonnay leads the whites, and Gewürztraminer and Sauvignon Blanc are small.

questions.q: Which ice-age floods spread the sands and gravels across the Columbia basin?
questions.exp: Repeated bursts of glacial Lake Missoula in Montana swept the basin at the end of the ice age, leaving the deep sands, silts and gravels that windblown loess later covered.
